newsitem.title: LATVIA: FOCUS - LITHUANIA INFLATION SHOWS SUCCESS OF POLICIES-IMF.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - LITHUANIA INFLATION SHOWS SUCCESS OF POLICIES-IMF.

text.p: Lithuania's steadily falling inflation rate reflects the success of the currency board and monetary policy, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Monday.

The country's statistics department said on Monday that consumer prices rose by 0.2 percent in June for a year-on-year inflation rate of 7.6 percent, the lowest recorded by any Baltic state since the three launched market reforms in 1991.
That compares with a year-on-year rate of 28.1 percent in Lithuania in June last year and hyper-inflation close to 1,200 percent in 1992.
But prudent monetary and fiscal policies must be maintained to keep a lid on inflation and prevent any threat to the country's economic recovery, IMF Lithuanian representative Domenico Fanizza said.
"The inflation rate shows that the currency board has been successful and the macroeconomic policies that have been pursued have been the right ones," Fanizza told Reuters.

Under Lithuania's currency board system, launched in 1994 with IMF blessing, the central bank guarantees that it will have one dollar in reserve for every four litas in circulation, freezing the exchange rate at that level.
The current government plans to scrap the system gradually over a period of two to three years. It says it will do nothing hasty to rattle currency markets or reignite inflation.
"It (inflation reduction) should remain a paramount policy of the government," Fanizza said.
Fanizza said inflation should keep declining even after the currency board is gone provided the government keeps a tight fiscal and monetary stance.
"Fiscal discipline is essential...the fiscal deficit must not be gapped by printing money," he said.
He added that there were few pressures expected on the country's economic horizon which would push inflation back up.
"A further adjustment in energy prices could contribute to higher inflation, but it would not push prices up too high," he said.
"Nor does there seem to be any concern that rising wages will lead to higher inflation," he said.
